messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 30
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Plumber
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 34

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Shouting: Shouting, Being Watched: Feeling watched or observed, Expressions of Anger: Other people expressing anger, even calmly
  Maladaptive Strategies: Undereating: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time
  Threat: Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
  Memory: Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing

Vignette:
Malia, a 30-year-old Māori woman, came to treatment after years of keeping her childhood largely sealed away behind work, marriage, and constant activity. She had grown up in a home where her caregiver’s moods could shift without warning, and the violence she later described was not a single dramatic incident but a pattern of being hit and intimidated in childhood when she was small enough to feel trapped and unable to leave. What stayed with her most was the sound of shouting and the sense of someone looming over her, watching to see whether she would flinch. When she recalled those years, she could only describe them in fragments: one moment a kitchen light, the hard edge of a bench, the sting of a hand; another moment a doorway, a raised voice, then nothing at all. Some parts of the event were extremely clear to her, but other stretches were blank, as if the memory had holes in it. She often said that what she remembered did not feel like her own past so much as something she had overheard about another child. The story belonged to someone else, she would think, and yet the images arrived with an upsetting vividness that made her stomach tighten.

As an adult, Malia built a life that seemed, on the surface, practical and steady. She worked as a plumber, spending her days in other people’s houses and on job sites, where she was often the only woman in the room. The work suited her in some ways because it was concrete and task-focused, but it also placed her in environments where she could not always control who stood behind her, who was looking at her hands, or how sharply someone might speak. Certain moments on the job would catch her off guard: a customer raising their voice over a misunderstanding, a supervisor speaking in an angry tone that others seemed to take as ordinary, or a colleague suddenly appearing beside her when she had thought she was alone. Even calm expressions of anger unsettled her. She would notice a tightened jaw, a clipped reply, a look that lasted too long, and her attention would narrow around it. At those times she felt as if she had to monitor the room for danger, not because she believed everyone was dangerous, but because her body behaved as if danger might be near. Unexpected movement beside her, especially in a cramped bathroom or under a sink, made her jerk back before she had time to think.

Over the years she responded by trying to keep herself occupied all the time. She filled every gap with work, chores, scrolling on her phone, or planning the next task, because quiet gave room for memories she did not want to face. She made a point of trying hard not to think about the trauma, pushing it away whenever it surfaced, though this left her feeling mentally crowded rather than rested. Eating became another area of control. Malia began restricting food without initially framing it as a symptom; she simply told herself she was too busy, not hungry, or did not have time to stop. In practice, undereating became part of how she managed the day, a way to keep herself contained and less open to whatever might come up if she slowed down. Over time, the pattern became more noticeable to her husband, who saw her skipping meals, drinking tea instead of eating, and becoming irritable when encouraged to sit down and share dinner. Their evenings, which had once been easy, increasingly revolved around her staying busy or retreating into practical tasks.

She described her body as living in a state of readiness she could not fully switch off. Even when nothing obvious was happening, her muscles stayed tense, as though braced for impact. At work she found it hard to concentrate for long, especially when there was noise, a raised voice, or people moving around her unexpectedly. She could complete jobs, but she often had to reread instructions or pause to collect herself because her mind would split between the task in front of her and the sensation that something might happen behind her. This constant alertness was exhausting, yet it also felt necessary to her, because when she let her guard drop she feared being caught off balance in the same helpless way she had been as a child.

By the time she sought help, Malia was no longer able to keep the old experiences compartmentalized. A recent series of encounters at work had left her increasingly unsettled, particularly one day when a customer began shouting over a delay and stepped into her path while gesturing angrily. She had done the job and left, but afterward she found herself replaying the scene and feeling ashamed that her body had reacted so strongly. She also noticed that she was increasingly avoiding meals and relying on staying busy to make it through the day. What finally brought her in was the sense that she was tired of living as though her own house, workplace, and even her own body might become places she had to defend. She hoped treatment might help her feel less on edge and more able to stay present, but what frightened her most was the possibility that the memories, with their missing pieces and strange, unclaimed quality, would keep intruding until she no longer felt at home in her own life.
